lessons.title: Early Hires, Advisors and Sweat Equity: Giving Away Equity Before You Raise

children.text: Before any investor arrives, a founder gives away equity four or five times. A first engineer who accepts a below-market salary. A design agency that offers to build the app for shares. A well-known operator who agrees to be an advisor and take calls once a month. Each conversation feels small. Added together they are often larger than the entire seed round's dilution, and unlike investor dilution, this kind buys no cash at all.

body.text: Pre-investor equity is the most expensive currency you have, because it is the cheapest one to hand out. Never pay in shares for something cash can buy, and never grant equity without vesting and a written instrument.

children.text: Four Ways to Give Someone Equity in India

"Give them 1%" is a sentence, not a structure. The Companies Act, 2013 offers a few distinct routes, and picking the wrong one creates tax bills, filing problems and disputes. Here is what each is for.

body.caption: Instruments for granting equity before a priced round

cells: Options granted from a pool, vesting over time, exercised later by paying the exercise price
Needs a formal plan, shareholder approval and a grant letter. Options are not shares until exercised
Directors and employees contributing know-how or intellectual property
Actual shares issued for non-cash consideration under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013
Statutory ceilings, valuation by a registered valuer and a lock-in period apply
Shares allotted and paid for at face value or an agreed price
Creates a tax question once a fair market value exists, and gives voting rights immediately
A small option grant from the same pool, vesting over one to two years
Advisors rarely deserve employee-sized grants. Keep the number small and time-bound

body.text: Sweat equity shares are tightly regulated. Under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the related rules, they can only go to directors or employees, must be valued by a registered valuer, carry a lock-in, and are capped as a percentage of paid-up equity capital, with a more generous ceiling available to startups recognised by DPIIT. For most early hires, ESOPs are simpler and cheaper to administer than sweat equity.

body.label: Startup India recognition (DPIIT)
body.description: DPIIT recognition unlocks several relaxations that matter for cap tables, including more generous sweat equity limits and the ability to grant ESOPs to promoters and large-shareholder directors for a defined period after incorporation.

children.text: Sizing the Pool Before You Start Granting

markDefs.definition: A block of shares reserved for future employee option grants. It appears on the fully diluted cap table as soon as it is created, even before a single option is granted.

children.text: , never ad hoc. MetroMandi has 10,000 founder shares and wants a pool that is exactly 10% of the company once created. That is not 1,000 options, because the pool has to dilute itself too.

content.caption: Sizing a pool to hit a target percentage of the enlarged company

children.text: 10,000 ÷ (1 - 0.10) = 11,111.11, rounded to 11,111 fully diluted shares. Pool = 11,111 - 10,000 = 1,111 options, which is 1,111 ÷ 11,111 = 10.00% of the enlarged company. If MetroMandi had simply reserved 1,000 options, the pool would have been 1,000 ÷ 11,000 = 9.09%, short of the target.
What Each Person Should Actually Get

These ranges are typical for early-stage Indian startups before a priced round. They are starting points for a conversation, not rules, and they should always be read alongside the cash salary being offered.

body.caption: Typical pre-seed grant ranges, fully diluted

cells: Head of a function, near-founder hire
Reserve the top of the range for someone taking a large pay cut
Scale with seniority and how much salary they are giving up
Below-market salary should be compensated in cash later, not only in options
Tie it to a defined commitment, such as monthly calls and two introductions a quarter
Pay cash. Equity for an agency is permanent payment for a temporary service

body.title: Size the pool
body.prompt: A Noida startup has 8,000 shares issued to its founders and wants an ESOP pool equal to 12% of the company after the pool is created. How many options should it reserve? Round to the nearest whole option.
body.explanation: 8,000 ÷ (1 - 0.12) = 9,090.9, so about 9,091 fully diluted shares. Pool = 9,091 - 8,000 = 1,091 options, which is 1,091 ÷ 9,091 = 12.00%. Reserving a flat 960 options, which is 12% of 8,000, would have produced a pool of only 10.71% of the enlarged company.

children.text: Equity Is Not a Substitute for Cash

body.title: Paying an early hire: cash vs equity

columns.label: What equity does well
points: Aligns someone with the long-term outcome
Costs no cash today, which matters when runway is short
Rewards people who take real career risk early
Is worth a great deal if the company succeeds

columns.label: What equity does badly
points: Pays nobody's rent or EMI this month
Is illiquid for years in an unlisted company
Is permanent, even when the contribution was temporary
Is usually overvalued by founders and undervalued by candidates

body.label: What 1% is actually worth
body.context: 1% of a company valued at ₹4.9 crore is ₹4.9 lakh, but it cannot be sold, it may be worth nothing, and the holder still has to pay the exercise price to convert options into shares. Say this out loud to candidates. A grant explained honestly is worth more than one oversold.

body.text: The most common pre-seed mistake is the casual advisor grant. A well-known name asks for 2% for "opening doors". Two percent is more than most first engineers get for four years of full-time work. If an advisor genuinely moves the needle, 0.25% to 0.5% over two years with quarterly vesting and a defined commitment is generous. Anything larger should be a job, not an advisory role.

body.title: Pick the right instrument
body.question: A former industry executive will advise your Mumbai healthtech startup for one day a month for two years. She is not an employee and will not take a salary. What is the cleanest way to give her equity?
options: Allot her equity shares immediately at face value
Issue her sweat equity shares under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013
Grant a small number of options from the ESOP pool, vesting quarterly over two years, under a written advisory agreement
Promise her 1% verbally and document it after the seed round closes
body.explanation: A time-bound option grant with quarterly vesting matches a time-bound commitment and costs nothing if the relationship ends early. Direct shares hand over voting rights and a permanent stake on day one. Sweat equity is limited to directors and employees and carries valuation and lock-in requirements. A verbal promise is the worst of all options, because it is undocumented dilution.

body.title: Name the reserve
body.textWithBlank: Shares set aside for future employee option grants, which count in the fully diluted total even before any option is granted, are called the ESOP ___.
body.explanation: The pool sits on the fully diluted cap table from the moment it is created, which is why creating a 10% pool dilutes the founders by 10 percentage points before any hire receives anything.

body.title: Three equity requests in one week
body.scenario: You run a pre-seed Ahmedabad SaaS startup with 10,000 founder shares and no ESOP pool. This week: a design agency offers to build your entire front end for 4% instead of its ₹12 lakh fee; a senior engineer will join full-time at a ₹10 lakh pay cut and asks for 2%; and a well-known founder offers to be an advisor for 1.5% because "that is what I take everywhere". You have ₹90 lakh in the bank and 14 months of runway.
body.prompt: How do you respond to each, and what do you set up first?
body.modelAnswer:
Set up first: an ESOP pool. Sizing a pool of about 10% before granting anything means 10,000 ÷ 0.9 = 11,111 fully diluted shares and a pool of 1,111 options. Every grant below comes out of that pool, under a written plan with a grant letter and vesting.

The agency: say no to equity, pay the ₹12 lakh. Four percent of a company that may one day be worth ₹500 crore is ₹20 crore for a piece of front-end work. You have 14 months of runway and this is exactly what cash is for. If cash is genuinely tight, negotiate staged payments, not shares.

The senior engineer: this is the request worth saying yes to. She is full-time, taking a ₹10 lakh annual pay cut and carrying real risk. Something in the 1% to 2% range, vesting over four years with a one-year cliff, is defensible. Offer to revisit cash compensation after the seed round so she is not being paid only in paper.

The advisor: counter at 0.25% to 0.5%, vesting quarterly over two years, with a written advisory agreement setting out what he will actually do, such as monthly calls and a set number of introductions. If 1.5% is non-negotiable for him, walk away. He is asking for roughly the same equity as a full-time senior hire for a fraction of the commitment.

The principle running through all three: equity is for people taking long-term risk alongside you. Everything else gets paid in rupees.

body.title: Before you promise anyone equity
steps: Ask whether cash could buy this instead. If it could, pay cash.
Create a properly approved ESOP plan and pool before the first grant, not after.
Size the pool using the enlarged-company formula so it hits the percentage you intended.
Express every grant as a number of options and a percentage of the fully diluted company, never as a vague percentage.
Attach vesting to every single grant, including advisors, with a cliff for employees.
Issue a written grant letter or advisory agreement, and record the grant on the cap table the same day.
Confirm the person is eligible for the instrument you are using, especially for sweat equity and for promoter-directors.
Track how much of the pool is left, so the next investor's top-up demand does not surprise you.

cards.definition: Shares reserved for future employee option grants, counted in the fully diluted total from the day the pool is created.
The document giving an employee a specific number of options, with exercise price, vesting schedule and expiry.
Shares issued under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013 to directors or employees for know-how or intellectual property, subject to valuation, ceilings and a lock-in.
The amount an option holder pays to convert a vested option into an actual share.
A small, time-bound option grant to a part-time advisor, usually vesting quarterly over one to two years.
Startup India recognition that unlocks relaxations, including more generous sweat equity ceilings and wider ESOP eligibility for a defined period.
Options reserved but not yet granted. Investors look at this number to judge whether you can hire without a top-up.

points: Founders usually give away more equity before their first round than in the round itself, and this dilution brings in no cash.
Match the instrument to the person: ESOPs for employees, small time-bound option grants for advisors, sweat equity only where Section 54 fits, direct shares only for genuine co-founders.
Size the pool with the enlarged-company formula. For 10,000 shares and a 10% target, the pool is 1,111 options, not 1,000.
Typical pre-seed ranges: 1% to 3% for a near-founder hire, 0.5% to 1.5% for a first engineer, 0.1% to 0.5% for early employees and advisors.
Agencies and vendors should be paid in cash. Equity is permanent payment for temporary work.
Every grant needs vesting, a written instrument and a same-day cap table entry.
Be honest about what a grant is worth: illiquid, uncertain, and payable only after the exercise price is paid.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. MetroMandi and the other startups and people described are fictional, and all option counts, percentages and ranges are illustrative rather than benchmarks. Eligibility rules, ceilings, approval requirements and lock-in periods for ESOPs and sweat equity shares are set by the Companies Act, 2013 and its rules and change over time, with separate treatment for DPIIT-recognised startups and for listed companies under SEBI regulations. Tax consequences for the recipient depend on the instrument and the facts. Work with a qualified company secretary and chartered accountant before creating a pool or issuing any shares.
